hints: Work backwards from benzoyl chloride, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$, and ask what functional group on the benzene ring can be converted into $\text{-COCl}$ in one step.
walkthrough:
See what must change at the side chain**
You start with $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and you finish with $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$. The benzene ring is unchanged, so all the chemistry happens on the side chain. The final carbon attached to the ring in benzoyl chloride is a carbonyl carbon bonded to Cl and O.

Spot the carboxylic acid link**
An acyl chloride $\text{-COCl}$ is almost always made from the corresponding carboxylic acid $\text{-COOH}$. So M must already have the $\text{-C=O}$ carbon attached directly to the ring, that is benzoic acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$.
Final answer: M is benzoic acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$ (benzene ring bonded directly to $\text{-COOH}$).

hints: Recall what happens when an alkyl side chain on benzene with benzylic hydrogens is heated with a very strong oxidiser.
Recall the specific chlorinating reagents that replace $\text{-OH}$ of a carboxylic acid by $\text{-Cl}$ without touching the benzene ring.
walkthrough:
Oxidise the whole ethyl side chain away**
Ethylbenzene has benzylic hydrogens, so vigorous oxidation cleaves the side chain completely to give $\text{-COOH}$ directly attached to the ring. Think hot, concentrated, alkaline $\text{MnO}_4^-$ with heating, followed by dilute acid to protonate the benzoate ion to benzoic acid.

Turn the acid into the acyl chloride**
Carboxylic acids do not react with $\text{HCl}$. You need a dedicated chlorinating agent. $\text{SOCl}_2$ is the cleanest choice, $\text{PCl}_5$ also works, giving $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl} + \text{SO}_2 + \text{HCl}$ for example. Heat is often used.

Final answer: step 1: hot alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$, heat, then acidify
step 2: $\text{SOCl}_2$ OR $\text{PCl}_5$ OR $\text{PCl}_3$, heat

hints: For step 1, track the oxidation number of the benzylic carbon from $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ to $\text{-COOH}$ and decide if oxygen content has increased.
For step 2, focus on what happens at the carbonyl carbon when $\text{-OH}$ is replaced by $\text{-Cl}$.
walkthrough:
Classify step 1 by oxygen gain**
Going from $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$ adds two oxygen atoms and removes hydrogens. Gain of oxygen and loss of hydrogen is oxidation. The benzene ring itself is not oxidised.

Classify step 2 by group swap**
Going from $\text{-COOH}$ to $\text{-COCl}$ swaps $\text{-OH}$ for $\text{-Cl}$ at the same carbonyl carbon. One nucleophile replaces another group, so this is nucleophilic substitution. At A Level you can simply call it substitution.

Final answer: step 1: oxidation
step 2: (nucleophilic) substitution

hints: Start with polarity in box one: which atom of $\text{C=O}$ in $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$ is $\delta+$ and which lone pair on phenol, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, will attack it.
Picture the first arrow from the phenol oxygen lone pair to the carbonyl carbon, paired with an arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ bond up onto oxygen to form the tetrahedral intermediate.
In box two, think how the intermediate collapses: which two bonds must break to reform $\text{C=O}$ and release chloride, and where does the $\text{O-H}$ proton go.
Balance atoms between box two and box three to work out the small second product alongside phenyl benzoate, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOC}_6\text{H}_5$.
walkthrough:
Set up the electrophile and nucleophile**
Look at benzoyl chloride. Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so label $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$. That $\delta+$ carbon is strongly electrophilic because it is joined to two electronegative atoms, O and Cl. Phenol attacks through a lone pair on its $\text{-OH}$ oxygen. Draw lone pairs on that O, on the carbonyl O, and on Cl.

Make the first bond and form the intermediate**
Draw a curly arrow starting at the phenol oxygen lone pair and pointing to the carbonyl $\text{C}^{\delta+}$. At the same time draw a second curly arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ double bond up onto the oxygen. The $\pi$ bond breaks, oxygen gains the electrons and becomes $\text{O}^-$, while the phenol oxygen that has donated its pair becomes $\text{O}^+$. You now have the tetrahedral intermediate in box two.

Collapse the intermediate to reform the carbonyl**
Now reverse the process. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on the $\text{O}^-$ back down to reform $\text{C=O}$. To keep carbon to four bonds, two leaving events happen: a curly arrow from the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond onto Cl to expel $\text{Cl}^-$, and a curly arrow from the $\text{O-H}$ bond onto the positively charged oxygen to release the proton. This restores neutral oxygen in the ester linkage.

Identify the second product**
Count atoms. The $\text{H}$ from phenol and the $\text{Cl}$ from the acyl chloride are left over. Together they form $\text{HCl}$. So box three contains phenyl benzoate, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C(=O)OC}_6\text{H}_5$, plus $\text{HCl}$.

Final answer: Box one: $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$ on benzoyl chloride; lone pairs on phenol O and on $\text{C=O}$ O and on Cl; curly arrow from phenol O lone pair to carbonyl C; curly arrow from $\text{C=O}$ bond to O.
Box two: tetrahedral intermediate with $\text{O}^+$ on former phenol O and $\text{O}^-$ on former carbonyl O; curly arrow $\text{O-H}$ to O; curly arrow $\text{C-Cl}$ to Cl; curly arrow from $\text{O}^-$ lone pair to reform $\text{C=O}$.
Box three: products are $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOC}_6\text{H}_5$ and $\text{HCl}$.

hints: Remember the two-stage name for attack on an acyl chloride that first adds to $\text{C=O}$ then ejects $\text{Cl}^-$.
walkthrough:
Name the two stages you just drew**
First the phenol added to the $\text{C=O}$ to give a tetrahedral intermediate, that is addition. Then $\text{HCl}$ was eliminated as $\text{C=O}$ reformed, that is elimination. Because the attacker is a nucleophile, the full name is nucleophilic addition-elimination.
Final answer: (nucleophilic) addition-elimination

hints: Recall the vigorous white fumes with benzoyl chloride in water versus the lack of reaction of chlorobenzene, to place the easiest and hardest ends of the order.

Compare the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond strength in $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ where a Cl lone pair can interact with the ring, with the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond next to $\text{C=O}$ in $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$.
Think about electron donation from the ethyl group in chloroethane versus electron withdrawal by $\text{C=O}$ in benzoyl chloride toward attack by water.
walkthrough:
State the observed order**
Picture adding each to cold water. Benzoyl chloride hydrolyses vigorously to benzoic acid and $\text{HCl}$. Chloroethane hydrolyses slowly on warming. Chlorobenzene shows no reaction even on boiling. So hardest is chlorobenzene, middle is chloroethane, easiest is benzoyl chloride.

Explain why chlorobenzene is so inert**
In chlorobenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$, a lone pair in a p-orbital on Cl overlaps and delocalises into the benzene $\pi$ ring. This gives the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond partial double bond character. It is shorter and stronger, so nucleophilic attack by water cannot easily break it.

Explain why benzoyl chloride is so reactive**
In benzoyl chloride, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$, the carbonyl carbon is bonded to O and Cl, both highly electronegative. The electron withdrawing $\text{C=O}$ makes that carbon strongly $\delta+$, a powerful electrophile for water. The $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is therefore weakened and easily broken on attack. Chloroethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, sits in between because the alkyl group donates electrons by the positive inductive effect, reducing the $\delta+$ on carbon compared with the acyl chloride, but it has no partial double bond strengthening like chlorobenzene.

Final answer: Order: chlorobenzene (hardest to hydrolyse) < chloroethane < benzoyl chloride (easiest to hydrolyse).
Chlorobenzene: Cl lone pair overlaps with benzene $\pi$ system, giving $\text{C-Cl}$ partial double bond character, stronger and harder to break.
Benzoyl chloride: carbonyl C is very $\delta+$ due to electron withdrawing $\text{C=O}$ with two electronegative atoms, so $\text{C-Cl}$ is weaker and attack by water is very easy; chloroethane is intermediate with electron donating alkyl group reducing $\delta+$ on C.
